title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

title: CYB2-knockout Saccharomyces cerevisiae exerts effective antibacterial activity via lactic acid accumulation
abstract: Bacterial infectious diseases pose a major threat to human health, and rising antibiotic resistance has complicated treatment. Probiotics are promising alternatives, but their mechanisms remain largely unclear. Here, we screened a randomly selected subset of 1,733 strains from the homozygous diploidgene-knockout collection (YKOC) and identified CYB2-knockout (CYB2-KO)as a strain with potent antibacterial activity. CYB2-KOeffectively inhibited the growth of pathogenic bacteria, including multidrug-resistant strains, and suppressed biofilm formation by reducing bacterial adhesion, EPS production, and cell surface hydrophobicity. It also increased bacterial cell wall and membrane permeability. The strain showed no hemolytic activity, tolerated acidic conditions and high bile salt concentrations, and exhibited superior auto-aggregation and co-aggregation with pathogenic bacteria. In mouse models of urinary tract infection and enteritis, CYB2-KOincreased survival and reduced bacterial counts in the bladder, ileum, colon, and cecum. Mechanistically,deletion led to lactic acid (LA) accumulation and environmental acidification. Dose-response experiments with exogenous LA, pH neutralization, and supplementation of BY4743 CFS with LA at the CFS-equivalent concentration provided direct causal evidence that LA is the key effector metabolite. These findings highlight CYB2-KOas a promising probiotic candidate with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, with LA accumulation as the primary mechanism underlying its therapeutic effects.

abstract: Spondylodiscitis is an uncommon spinal infection that remains diagnostically challenging because of its non-specific symptoms and radiological overlap with tuberculosis and neoplasms. Among these, infections caused byare extremely unusual, and the case becomes even more challenging when multidrug resistance (MDR) is present. We describe a 49-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension who presented with persistent back pain following an episode of enteric fever. Imaging showed spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, initially suspected as tuberculosis or metastasis. A mammogram and tuberculosis (TB) workup were negative. Definitive diagnosis was only achieved during surgery. Intraoperative biopsy and culture confirmed, resistant to multiple antibiotics but sensitive to imipenem and azithromycin. Targeted therapy led to clinical improvement. This case underlines the diagnostic difficulty of spinal infections, where radiology alone cannot differentiate between infection and malignancy. Surgical biopsy and culture remain essential, aligning with current Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommendations. Multidrug-resistantspondylodiscitis is exceptionally rare. Early tissue diagnosis and tailored therapy are key to achieving favorable outcomes.

title: How do domiciliary carers contribute to preventing the spread of antimicrobial resistance? A qualitative study in England
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global problem that requires coordinated action. Most antibiotics in England are used in community settings, giving all community health and care professionals potentially important roles in antimicrobial stewardship (AMS). Currently little evidence exists on how the adult social care workforce, including domiciliary carers providing care at home, contribute to AMS, despite the unique opportunities of their role. To explore domiciliary care workers' knowledge of AMR and identify existing contributions and opportunities to improve AMS. We used a purposive sampling approach to recruit a diverse sample of domiciliary carers working in England and administered a semi-structured interview exploring their views and practices relating to AMS. Thematic analysis was applied. We interviewed 30 domiciliary carers. Analysis of participants' responses indicated that carers supported AMS in the following ways: infection prevention and control (IPC), and signposting clients to healthcare and antibiotic administration. However, carers generally did not recognize themselves as actively contributing to AMS. We identified unrecognized areas of good AMS practice, along with opportunities to enhance domiciliary carers' impact on AMS. Potential interventions include improving timeliness of adding antibiotics to care plans as well as inclusion of AMS behaviours in them, co-developing training with carers on AMR to reinforce their AMS practices, clear distinction of carers' contributions as part of a whole-system approach to tackling AMR, and embedding AMS competencies into the Care Certificate for greater reach and consistency.

title: Engineered bacteriophages as precision antimicrobials against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: molecular engineering strategies, clinical translation, and the crystallizing global regulatory landscape
abstract: The global antimicrobial resistance crisis, driven primarily by the ESKAPE pathogen consortium has catalyzed the translation of engineered bacteriophage therapeutics from experimental platforms to clinical-stage precision medicines. Unlike their wild-type counterparts, which are constrained by narrow host ranges, susceptibility to reticuloendothelial clearance, and limited biofilm penetrability, synthetically engineered phages exploit receptor-binding protein remodeling, phage-derived enzymatic depolymerases, CRISPR-Cas3 chromosomal shredding payloads, sequence-independent SASPject delivery vectors, and in vivo microbiome base editors to overcome the multilayered resistance arsenals of MDR ESKAPE organisms. Recent clinical development has generated human evidence across both genetically engineered phage platforms and advanced fixed phage-cocktails. Engineered programmes include CRISPR-Cas3-based LBP-EC01 and SNIPR001, while AP-SA02 represents an analytically characterized fixed multi-phage cocktail targeting. This review examines engineering strategies, pharmacokinetics, immune-mediated clearance, delivery challenges, clinical evidence, manufacturing, and regulatory pathways. It also discusses emerging regulatory approaches and distinctions between natural and genetically modified phage products. The literature search was conducted from January-June 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, supplemented by searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and the websites of the US-FDA and EMA. Overall, this review evaluates the translational potential of engineered phages, identifies barriers to clinical adoption, and considers future developments in precision antimicrobial therapy against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

Five years of wastewater surveillance reveal COVID-19-Associated amplification and seasonal shifts in bla (KPC) and bla (NDM)
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Genetic diversity and resistance profiles of MRSA in community and healthcare settings
abstract: This study aimed to characterize and compare methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains isolated from community members and healthcare workers (HCWs) in Egypt using antibiotic susceptibility testing, mecA gene detection, SCCmec typing, and ERIC-PCR fingerprinting. A cross-sectional study was conducted between September 2024 and January 2025, during which 450 specimens were collected from Mansoura University Hospitals and the local community, where 71 specimens (30.8%) were confirmed as MRSA. MRSA prevalence was significantly higher among HCWs, 62.5% (50/80), than among community members, 14% (21/150). In general, antibiotic resistance rates were higher in HCW strains. All isolates were resistant to cefoxitin and sensitive to vancomycin.The methicillin-resistant phenotype of the 71 MRSA isolates was confirmed by positive mecA gene tests, with SCCmec Type III prevalent among healthcare workers and SCCmec Type IV predominating in the community. ERIC-PCR fingerprinting demonstrated the isolates' genetic diversity. The dendrogram based on ERIC patterns showed distinct clusters between community and hospital strains, though with some overlap, suggesting possible transmission between the two populations.In conclusion, MRSA strains from HCWs displayed broader antibiotic resistance and greater clonal similarity, while community strains were more diverse and less resistant. The presence of intermixed clusters between community-acquired (CA-MRSA) and (HCW-MRSA) suggested a possible bidirectional transmission pathway, underscoring the blurring of epidemiological boundaries.These results underline the necessity of ongoing molecular surveillance and integrated infection control strategies to track the spread of MRSA in community and clinical settings.

title: Discovery and development of antimicrobial polymers
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is among the most pressing healthcare challenges of our time. Multidrug-resistant 'superbugs' continue to emerge at an alarming rate, while antibiotic development has stalled in recent decades. Antimicrobial peptides have attracted interest for their potent bactericidal activity and lower propensity to spur resistance; however, translation into clinical practice has been hampered by poor bioavailability, challenging syntheses and limited stability. By contrast, synthetic copolymers mimicking antimicrobial peptides have received attention for their efficacy and synthetic tractability. Here we highlight recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discuss future directions for their design and implementation. We also outline future research directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods that ensure the worldwide accessibility of these materials.

title: Neonatal sepsis
abstract: Neonatal sepsis and preterm birth are leading contributors to childhood death and disability in sepsis survivors. Whereas deaths from infectious diseases of childhood have declined substantially worldwide, progress in reducing neonatal sepsis burden and impact has stagnated in many low-income and middle-income countries. Efforts to track and prevent neonatal sepsis are hampered by the lack of a universally accepted case definition, gaps in global surveillance programmes, varied clinical presentations, and paucity of accurate and affordable sepsis diagnostics. The changing epidemiology of neonatal sepsis with predominance of Gram-negative pathogens, antimicrobial resistance, scarcity of and inequitable access to novel antibiotics, and under-representation of neonates in antibiotic clinical trials, are key issues impeding optimal treatment. Research and programmatic interventions to accelerate neonatal sepsis prevention and treatment should be prioritized alongside preterm birth prevention. Key actions include improving clinical care and infection prevention practices, and developing new diagnostic tests and vaccines that target the most common neonatal sepsis pathogens, particularly those responsible for the greatest morbidity and mortality.

title: Beyond the worm: engineering the next generation of nematode-inspired antimicrobials
abstract: The global crisis of multidrug-resistant bacteria and parasitic nematodes demands new approaches to infectious disease control. Emerging evidence suggests that gastrointestinal nematodes and the host gut microbiota are inextricably linked in a complex 'holobiont'. Parasitic nematodes have evolved in microbe-rich environments for millennia, developing innate immune defenses. This evolutionary 'arms race' has produced a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that can target bacteria and other gut microbiota. With over 5000 AMP and AMP-like domain-encoding genes identified via computational mining, the bottleneck is validation. The integration of machine learning algorithms with advanced in vitro and ex vivo models will allow prediction of AMP mode of action, spectrum of activity, and efficacy, followed by testing in organoids to address some of the limitations of animal models.

title: Helicobacter pylori antibiotic resistance in Egypt exceeds eradication thresholds: systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Eradicating Helicobacter pylori in Egypt is severely hindered by escalating antibiotic resistance. Comprehensive national resistance data are essential for optimizing failing treatment protocols. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the pooled prevalence of Helicobacter pylori resistance to key antibiotics in Egypt to inform national treatment guidelines. Data sources: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Egyptian Knowledge Bank (EKB). Primary studies published between 2000 and 2025 reporting H. pylori antibiotic resistance prevalence in Egypt were included. Human subjects with documented H. pylori infection. Resistance was assessed for metronidazole, amoxicillin, clarithromycin, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolones. Assessment of risk of bias: The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prevalence Studies was used. Methods of data synthesis: Pooled prevalence and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a random-effects model with Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation. Thirty studies comprising 5019 observations were included. The resistance rate for clarithromycin was 42.8% (95% CI: 34.7-51.1%), nearly tripling the 15% Maastricht clinical threshold for abandoning empirical clarithromycin-containing regimens. Rates for other primary antibiotics were also critically high: metronidazole 79.1% (95% CI: 64.7-90.8%) and amoxicillin 45.8% (95% CI: 29.1-62.9%), both far exceeding rates typical for standard empirical therapies. Resistance to tetracycline (23.4%), ciprofloxacin (20.0%), and levofloxacin (18.8%) also surpassed clinical cutoffs. Significant geographic disparities were observed across governorates, with metronidazole resistance reaching 100% in some regions. Meta-regression indicated that these high resistance levels have remained stable over the past two decades. Egypt Delta and the Cairo metropolitan areas face a critical burden of Helicobacter pylori resistance, rendering standard empirical triple therapies suboptimal. National guidelines should prioritise quadruple therapy or susceptibility-guided treatments to improve eradication outcomes. PROSPERO (CRD420251249967).

title: Streptococcus thoraltensis in a Postoperative Wound Infection and a Therapeutic Regimen Associated with Successful Eradication
abstract: is commonly isolated from swine and rabbits; however, over the past decade, it has caused various infections in human beings. The treatment of these infections is typically complex because of an association with antibiotic resistance. A 20-year-old female patient presented with a postoperative surgical site infection and a positive culture for, representing a clinical combination not previously described. A favorable response was achieved by implementing a treatment regimen based on surgical wound cleansing with an isotonic and stabilized 0.057% sodium hypochlorite antimicrobial solution, followed by the application of a gel of the same composition, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, and the use of a Negative Pressure Wound Therapy. The relevance of this case lies in its presentation of a new clinical manifestation of the infection, marking the third report and fifth case described within the Mexican population. Above all, it outlines a therapeutic protocol that achieved favorable outcomes, providing a valuable reference for future cases.

title: Genomic profiling of maternal Streptococcus agalactiae reveals prophage-associated resistance and comparative characterization of anovaginal and respiratory isolates
authors: de Abreu Pereira MDC et al.
abstract: Maternal colonization with Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS) is a major risk factor for neonatal diseases. While anovaginal screening is the primary guide for antibiotic prophylaxis, the upper respiratory tract is an understudied potential reservoir for GBS disease. However, the maternal carriage, serotype distribution, and genetic determinants of respiratory colonization remain unknown. To investigate the prevalence and genomic determinants of antimicrobial resistance and virulence in anovaginal and nasal GBS carriage among pregnant women using molecular methods and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Paired nasal and anovaginal swabs were collected from 221 pregnant women. Colonization and capsular serotypes were detected using cfb- and cps-targeted qPCR, along with standard culture. Subsequently, the recovered isolates were subjected to antimicrobial susceptibility testing and WGS for pan-genomic and phylogenomic analyses. The overall GBS colonization prevalence was 24%, comprising 22.6% anovaginal and 2.3% nasal carriers. Notably, 49% of the positive samples were detected exclusively by qPCR, which also revealed multi-serotype co-colonization in 7.5% of the colonized women. Serotypes Ia and V were the most prevalent. Erythromycin resistance reached 31%, largely associated with a prophage harboring mefA-msrD within Tn1207.1. WGS revealed CC23 as the major lineage, which clustered with the nasal isolates. Furthermore, an exploratory hypothesis-generating pangenome analysis, suggested a potential association between respiratory isolates and a prophage encoding stress-response gene. Molecular screening outperformed standard culture, revealing hidden epidemiological complexities, including underreported co-colonization. The high prevalence of macrolide resistance associated with prophage-borne genes highlights the need for continuous genomic surveillance to track potentially emerging GBS lineages in maternal care.

title: State of the Art of Treatment of Acinetobacter baumannii Infections
abstract: complex is the most commonly identified group of species within the genusand has globally emerged as a major health care-associated pathogen.is the species most frequently responsible for human infections and has been classified by the World Health Organization as a critical-priority pathogen because of its remarkable ability to acquire antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and the high attributable mortality associated with its infections, which can reach 70% in critically ill patients. This section reviews the global and regional epidemiology of, its complex mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance, and current therapeutic strategies, with particular emphasis on newly approved antimicrobial agents.

title: Comparative Analysis of Phenotypic Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance Among Aeromonas veronii Strains Isolated from Different Farmed Freshwater Fish
abstract: is an important zoonotic pathogen causing severe diseases and high mortality in freshwater aquaculture. In this study, five strains (LY-3, JY-1, G7, G8, and WL-3) were isolated from different diseased freshwater fish in Linyi City, Shandong Province, China, and identified asusing phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA andB sequences. Five strains grew at 20-40°C, pH 5.0-8.0, and 0-3% NaCl, demonstrating strong environmental tolerance. Their optimal temperature and pH were identical, but optimal NaCl concentration was strain-dependent. Despite harboring the hemolysin-related genes,, and, all strains except JY-1 exhibited β-hemolytic activity. All strains exhibited distinct flagella-driven motility abilities. Specifically, only strain G8 possessed two polar flagella and exhibited the strongest swimming motility. Similarly, all strains formed biofilms, correlating with the production of N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL). Worryingly, all strains exhibited multi-drug resistance to three penicillin-class antibiotics, midecamycin, clindamycin, three carbapenems, vancomycin, and polymyxin B. Additionally, five strains carriedandgenes, and four strains (excluding LY-3) additionally harbored thegene. Encouragingly, most of isolates remained susceptible to florfenicol and enrofloxacin. These results indicate considerable intra-specific heterogeneity amongstrains from different geographical origins and host sources, suggesting an urgent need for precise treatments.

title: Exploring the potential of herbal nanotechnology for the treatment of urinary tract infections
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) continue to pose a substantial clinical challenge due to high recurrence, biofilm-mediated persistence, and the rapid expansion of antimicrobial resistance. The waning effectiveness of conventional antibiotics highlights the urgency for resistance-sparing therapeutic strategies. Recent advances in herbal nanotechnology have enabled the precise nanoengineering of plant-derived phytochemicals, enhancing their stability, bioavailability, and pathogen-specific activity. This review critically appraises nanomaterial-based phytotherapeutic approaches for UTI management, focusing on the mechanistic integration of phytochemical bioactivity with nanoscale delivery systems. Nanomaterials developed from medicinal plants, crude extracts, and isolated phytoconstituents are evaluated for their ability to interfere with uropathogen adhesion, dismantle biofilms, suppress virulence signaling, induce oxidative stress, and regulate host inflammatory responses. Translational barriers, including formulation reproducibility, safety assessment, scalable production, and regulatory compliance, are also examined. By consolidating antimicrobial, antibiofilm, and host-modulatory evidence, this review identifies nano-enabled phytotherapeutic strategies with translational promise as multi-target alternatives to antibiotic-based UTI therapy.

title: One health molecular epidemiology of carbapenem- and colistin-resistant Escherichia coli sequence types in humans, poultry, and the environment in Pakistan
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is a grave One Health concern, leading to increased mortality and economic loss globally. These pathogens have acquired several resistance genes against WHO-defined medically important classes of antibiotics. Therefore, we plan to investigate AMR prevalence within the One Health framework. A total of 300 samples (100 each from human clinical, poultry, and environmental sources) were collected aseptically. We cultured isolates using standard microbiological methods and identified them with the VITEK2 Compact system. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Two-locus CH typing was used to assign sequence types (STs), and PCR was performed to detect bla, bla, bla, bla, and mcr-1. A total of 27 carbapenem-resistant E. coli (CR-EC) and 3 colistin-resistant E. coli (ColR-EC) isolates were recovered from human samples, 38 CR-EC and 5 ColR-EC from environmental samples, and 25 ColR-EC from poultry samples. Among all isolates, ST101 (21/90; 23.3%), ST131 (15/90; 16.7%), and ST405 (15/90; 16.7%) were the predominant sequence types. All three reservoirs harboured ST101, ST131, and ST405, while ST648 was shared between human and environmental isolates, and ST10 was shared between poultry and environmental isolates. Among environmental carbapenem-resistant isolates, bla(20/38; 52.6%), bla(18/38; 47.4%), bla(11/38; 28.9%), bla(6/38; 15.8%), and mcr-1 (5/38; 13.2%) were detected. All human carbapenem-resistant isolates carried bla(27/27; 100%), whereas all poultry colistin-resistant isolates harboured mcr-1 (25/25; 100%). High-risk multidrug-resistant E. coli lineages carrying carbapenemase and colistin resistance genes are widely distributed across human, poultry, and environmental reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Molecular characterization of virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance determinants in Arcobacter butzleri isolated from seafood of the Mumbai coast, India
abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the occurrence of Arcobacter butzleri in seafood from the Mumbai coast, India and evaluated its genetic potential associated with virulence and antimicrobial resistance through comprehensive analysis of virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. Among the 70 samples screened, 44 were positive for A. butzleri, resulting in an overall prevalence of 62.86%. A higher rate of prevalence was reported from bivalves (84.62%), followed by crustaceans (78.57%), finfish (60.61%) and cephalopods (33.33%). Characterization of isolates based on putative virulence-associated genes revealed that most of them harboured more than five genes. Genes such as tlyA, cadF, ciaB, mviN and pldA were found dominant, whereas irgA and hecA were the limiting ones. Sample level characterization of total number of virulence-associated genes yielded significant differences among the seafood categories tested, with significant association between iroE gene and the sample category (P < 0.05). Phenotypic analysis of antibiotic susceptibility revealed 88.1% of the isolates to be multidrug resistant, with an average MAR indices of 0.39. The β-lactam resistant gene (bla) was found to be the dominant gene in the present study, followed by macA. This study, underscores the significance of seafood as a possible carrier of pathogenic and antimicrobial-resistant A. butzleri and emphasizes the need for continuous surveillance and implementation of stringent hygienic practices.

title: De Novo Design of Multi-Mechanistic AIE Photosensitizer for Broad-Spectrum Bacterial Eradication
abstract: Antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to human health. Inspired by the clinical practice of employing drug combinations to achieve combined effects, we hypothesized that integrating multiple mechanisms into a single molecule could address drug-resistant bacterial infections. Based on a propeller-modification strategy and dual alkyl-chain engineering, we de novo designed and synthesized a C2-symmetric propeller-shaped aggregation-induced emission photosensitizer. After iterative screening, the optimized compound MeOTDP-2 exhibits broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, enabling efficient eradication of planktonic bacteria, drug-resistant strains, polymicrobial infections, biofilms, and persister cells, with no cellular invasiveness and negligible cytotoxicity. Mechanistic studies revealed that MeOTDP-2 achieves chemo-photodynamic combined antibacterial therapy by targeting and disrupting bacterial membranes and DNA, alongside light-mediated intracellular reactive oxygen species accumulation. Furthermore, in mouse models of MRSA-induced skin abscess and full-thickness skin wound infection, MeOTDP-2 demonstrated superior therapeutic efficacy to vancomycin. This strategy, integrating dual targeting with multiple mechanisms, offers new promise for overcoming bacterial resistance.

title: Nucleic Acid Aptamers in Bacteriology: Mapping the Landscape, Exploring Bioimaging Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is becoming increasingly widespread, underlining the importance of rapid, accurate identification of bacterial infections for effective diagnostic, clinical, and environmental management. While next-generation sequencing excels at genetic characterization, it falls short in real-time, in situ detection, a critical gap where nucleic acid aptamers emerge as a compelling alternative. These synthetic oligonucleotides enable direct, low-cost, and versatile detection of bacterial targets without requiring DNA extraction or amplification. Their portability supports point-of-care diagnostics, while their molecular precision enables integration into advanced bioimaging platforms for non-invasive, real-time, spatial, and functional monitoring of pathogens in biological environments. This perspective explores the potential of aptamers for bacterial bioimaging, assessing the landscape of bacterial-targeting aptamers, zooming in on aptamer-based bioimaging approaches for bacterial detection, addressing key challenges, and outlining future opportunities, such as real-time dynamic infection imaging and theranostics, polyclonal/multivalent aptamers, multiplex imaging, aptamer-based biosensors, and AI-driven detection.

title: Spatiotemporal recurrence and dissemination of Salmonella subpopulations in surface waters of central Chile
abstract: Agricultural waters have been identified as one of the primary sources ofcontamination, which has resulted in numerous outbreaks associated with the consumption of contaminated produce. Consequently, an improved understanding ofcontamination of agricultural waters could facilitate the development of control strategies to prevent food contamination. The objective of this study was to examine the diversity and spatiotemporal recurrence ofisolates in surface water related to agricultural activities. Water samples (= 2,690) were collected between 2019 and 2024 in central Chile using modified Moore swabs, and whole-genome sequencing was carried out for 1 to 10isolates per sample. Non-clonal genomes from each sample (= 1,034) were analyzed, showing that the most frequently identified serovars were Infantis (14.6%), Typhimurium (10.8%), Newport (8.5%), and Enteritidis (5.8%). The highest antimicrobial resistance burden was shown byInfantis, which carried up to 11 antimicrobial resistance genes simultaneously. Importantly, phylogenomic analyses revealed a highly clonal population structure among the most prevalent serovars and identified recurrent subpopulations that were repeatedly detected across multiple watersheds and consecutive years, including lineages associated with human infections. These findings provide genomic evidence that agricultural surface waters may serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrentsubpopulations in central Chile, including multidrug-resistant strains. Our work underscores the critical importance of continuous environmental surveillance and the integration of environmental and clinical genomic surveillance data to improve our understanding of theecology and inform evidence-based mitigation strategies aiming to protect public health.IMPORTANCEis a leading cause of foodborne illness worldwide, and contaminated irrigation water is an important pathway by which this pathogen can reach fresh produce. By analyzing more than 1,000genomes collected from agricultural waters in central Chile over 5 years, we found that specific bacterial lineages persisted across multiple watersheds and years, including multidrug-resistant strains linked to human infections. These findings indicate that agricultural surface waters in Chile can serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrentsubpopulations. Our study highlights the value of continuous environmental surveillance and the need to integrate data from environmental and human sources to identify potential contamination sources and reduce the risk of foodborne disease.

title: Dynamics of within-host genomic relatedness and emergence of resistance in serial Mycobacterium avium complex isolates during treatment
abstract: complex infections require prolonged multidrug therapy and may develop antimicrobial resistance. We applied whole-genome sequencing (WGS) to assess within-patient genomic relatedness and resistance-associated mutations emerging during therapy. WGS was performed on cultured populations of 30 serial isolates (16and 14) from 13 patients with repeated recovery of the same species. Genomic relatedness was classified by species/subspecies, sequence type (ST), and fastBAPS (FB) clustering. Resistance-associated mutations were assessed in isolates showing susceptible-to-resistant conversion or an increase of at least two dilutions in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Among 13 patients, 10 (76.9%) showed concordant genomic patterns, 2 (15.4%) showed discordant genomic patterns with genetically distinct cultured populations, and 1 (7.7%) showed both concordant and discordant relationships across intervals. Sixteencultured populations belonged to four STs (ST112 and ST118, 75.0%) and four FB clusters. Fourteencultured populations belonged to four STs, predominantly ST1109 (71.4%). While most cultured populations of the same ST matched the same FB,ST112 and ST118 andST1109 each occurred in two FB clusters. Conversely, three STs (ST112, ST118, and ST1112) ofbelonged to the same FB. Among three cases with emergent clarithromycin resistance,mutations (A2058C and A2059G) were identified in two. In one case, anintergenic variant showed stepwise increases in variant allele frequency, accompanied by increasing ethambutol MICs. WGS provided two methods for analyzing within-patient genomic relatedness (ST assignment and FB clustering), which were mutually complementary and enabled longitudinal detection of resistance-associated mutations during treatment. complex pulmonary disease often requires prolonged multidrug therapy, during which serial culture-positive isolates may differ in within-patient genomic relatedness and antimicrobial resistance. Distinguishing closely related from genetically distinct isolates and identifying emerging resistance are clinically important but cannot be reliably achieved using conventional species identification or sequence typing alone. In this study, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of serialcomplex isolates enabled high-resolution assessment of within-patient genomic relatedness. WGS also identified emerging resistance-associated mutations, including acquiredmutations associated with high-level clarithromycin resistance during macrolide-containing therapy and anintergenic variant accompanying increasing ethambutol minimum inhibitory concentrations during ethambutol-containing treatment. These findings support the potential clinical utility of WGS for characterizing genomic relationships among recurrentcomplex isolates and detecting emergence of resistance-associated mutations during therapy.

title: Draft genome sequence of Enterococcus faecalis strain MBBL_RBS1 isolated from a dairy cow with repeat breeding syndrome
abstract: We report the draft genome ofstrain MBBL_RBS1, isolated from uterine discharge of a repeat-breeder dairy cow in Bangladesh. The 2.740 Mbp genome comprises 25 contigs, with 37.5% GC content, 6 antimicrobial resistance genes, 24 virulence genes, and a PathogenFinder-predicted probability of human pathogenicity of 0.889.

title: Pathogen identification and resistance gene expression tests using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension in gram-negative contrived positive blood cultures
abstract: Rapid pathogen identification, resistance detection, and susceptibility profiling improve antimicrobial prescribing and associated outcomes, but fragmented workflows lead to inefficiencies and are costly. We evaluated a research-use-only (RUO) approach using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension from routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) for matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) pathogen identification and lateral flow assay (LFA)-based detection of targeted resistance mechanisms. Gram-negative bacterial strains from reference and curated resistance collections (CDC1, ARLG2, and ATCC3) (= 129) were contrived into blood culture bottles and processed in the ASTar System using the ASTar BC G- Kit (Q-linea AB, Sweden). Under RUO conditions, remnant bacterial suspensions were collected ~1-2 h after ASTar run initiation and analyzed using NG Test CTX-M Multi, NG Test CARBA-5, NG Test Acineto-5 RUO, and MALDI-TOF MS. Mean (±SD) remnant suspension volume was 2,722 μL (±300 µL). All samples yielded high-confidence MALDI-TOF MS scores (>2.0), with five initially scoring <2.0 and resolving on repeat testing. LFA results showed full agreement with reference isolates forpositive/negative (32/32) and with 60 or 61 target carbapenemase-positive/negative isolates. Testing of a subset of samples to mimic reflex workflows with ASTar phenotypic results did not affect LFA performance (= 35; 23 Enterobacterales, 3, and 9). Cost savings can be realized versus commercial multiplex PCR. This integrated approach of ~6 h rapid phenotypic AST with same-run identification and resistance detection (1-2 h from instrument start) or reflex testing upon availability of ASTar results may support earlier susceptibility results and offer cost savings to current workflows.IMPORTANCERapid, integrated diagnostic workflows are recommended and essential for improving patient outcomes in bloodstream infections, where delays in pathogen identification and resistance detection can compromise timely antimicrobial therapy. Current workflows often rely on multiple platforms, increasing turnaround time and laboratory burden. Additionally, the clinical impact of rapid diagnostic results is dependent on timely interpretation and implementation within antimicrobial stewardship frameworks, which may involve complex decision algorithms. This study demonstrates that remnant bacterial suspensions generated during routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) using the ASTar System can be recovered and utilized for rapid matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry and lateral flow assay-based resistance detection. By enabling pathogen identification and/or resistance detection within ~1-2 h of AST initiation or resistance detection via reflex testing, this approach reduces duplicate sample testing and may enable earlier access to rapid microbiological results.

title: The wild avian resistome: metagenomic insights into antimicrobial resistance ecology
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in wild birds is increasingly studied as an ecological component of the wider One Health resistome, yet the evidentiary meaning of a resistance gene detected in avian material varies markedly with study design. This review synthesizes culture-based, whole-genome and metagenomic evidence with emphasis on what modern sequencing can and cannot establish about acquisition, persistence, mobility and transmission. Wild birds encounter antimicrobial-resistant bacteria and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through wastewater, landfills, livestock-associated environments, surface waters, sediments and food webs; resident synanthropic species can be as informative as long-distance migrants. Shotgun and genome-resolved metagenomics have expanded the known avian resistome, enabled host assignment and revealed links with mobile genetic elements and viromes, but DNA detection alone does not demonstrate viable carriage or directional dissemination. We therefore organize the evidence through an evidence-to-inference framework of five complementary domains: ARG detection, microbial-host assignment, genomic mobility, viable carriage and persistence, and transmission, the last separated into sharing between compartments and direction of movement. Applying the framework to published sequencing studies shows that most reach only detection or host assignment, rely on relative abundance, rarely report negative controls and come predominantly from China. The framework clarifies why wild birds are often best regarded as ecological sentinels unless persistence, viable hosts and directionality are shown. Combining metagenomics with long-read sequencing, targeted culture, isolate genomics, environmental sampling and movement ecology offers the strongest route toward biologically meaningful One Health surveillance.

title: Development and clinical validation of a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing panel for simultaneous DNA/RNA pathogen detection in respiratory tract infections: a comprehensive performance evaluation
abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with approximately 62 % of cases lacking definitive etiological diagnoses via conventional methods. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing (mp-tNGS) panel for comprehensive pathogen detection in respiratory samples. We conducted a combined retrospective (n=209) and prospective (n=256) study involving 465 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples from patients with suspected LRTI. The mp-tNGS panel was designed to detect 277 clinically relevant pathogens, integrating simultaneous DNA/RNA co-detection and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based contamination control. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against conventional microbiological tests (CMTs) and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). The mp-tNGS assay revealed a limit of detection (LoD) of 25 copies/mL for bacteria/fungi and 50 copies/mL for viruses, with acceptable precision (intrabatch CV=9.42 %; interbatch CV=26.03 %). A novel SNP-based bioinformatics pipeline achieved exceptional discriminative performance (AUC=0.992) for distinguishing true infections from contamination. Compared with CMTs and mNGS, mp-tNGS showed superior sensitivity (93.59 %, 95 % CI: 90.81-95.73 %), particularly for viruses (AUC=0.92 vs. 0.845). The assay reliably identified fastidious pathogens (e.g.,and) and predicted antimicrobial resistance (97.08 % concordance with phenotypic testing). We developed an mp-tNGS panel with diagnostic performance comparable to that of mNGS. The panel integrates broad pathogen coverage, rapid turnaround time, machine learning-based false-positive reduction, and concordance with phenotypic susceptibility testing, positioning it as a promising molecular diagnostic tool for LRTI.

title: Vaginal and uterine volatile organic compound profiles, bacterial isolates, and antimicrobial susceptibility in canine pyometra
abstract: Canine pyometra is a life-threatening uterine disease requiring timely diagnosis and appropriate antimicrobial treatment. This study characterized uterine bacteria and antimicrobial susceptibility and compared vaginal and uterine volatile organic compound (VOC) profiles in 27 bitches with pyometra (14 open-cervix, 13 closed-cervix) and 14 healthy controls. Uterine isolates were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion. Vaginal and uterine swabs were analyzed by headspace solid-phase microextraction-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Aerobic bacterial growth occurred in 17/27 pyometra cases (63.0%), yielding nine species; Escherichia coli was most frequent (4/17 isolates; 23.5%).
