Chloramphenicol had the highest proportion of susceptible isolates (94.1%), whereas cephalexin had the highest resistance proportion (58.8%); one E. coli isolate was multidrug resistant. Among eight shared VOC features, VOC-1 and VOC-2 had greater peak areas in vaginal (P = 0.004 and 0.005) and uterine (P = 0.002 and 0.001) pyometra samples than controls. VOC-3 differed significantly only in uterine samples (P = 0.009). However, vaginal VOC-1, VOC-2, and VOC-3 did not significantly distinguish closed-cervix pyometra from healthy controls. Compound assignments were tentative (Metabolomics Standards Initiative Level 2/3), based on library matches without confirmation using authentic standards. These exploratory findings characterize uterine bacterial isolates, antimicrobial susceptibility, and vaginal and uterine VOC profiles in canine pyometra. Chemical confirmation and validation in larger independent cohorts are required before diagnostic application, particularly in closed-cervix cases.

title: Identification, Antimicrobial Susceptibility Profiling, and Genomic Characterization of Aeromonas Species Isolated from Cultured Freshwater Fish in Pakistan
abstract: Globally, Aeromonas infections pose a significant threat to the aquaculture sector and food security because of associated disease and production losses. In this study, different Aeromonas isolates were identified from the diseased fish. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) based analysis was used for phenotypic identification. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed to determine the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of the tested antimicrobial agents using the broth microdilution method. Genome sequencing was performed to characterize the Aeromonas isolates and identify virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified six Aeromonas species among 18 isolates, while one isolate remained unresolved at the species level. A. veronii (27.8%, 5/18) and A. dhakensis (22.2%, 4/18) were the most frequently detected species. MALDI-TOF MS correctly identified the isolates at the genus level but showed limited accuracy at the species level, particularly for A. dhakensis. Most isolates had allelic profiles that were not assigned to existing sequence types in the PubMLST database. Chromosomally encoded β-lactamase genes were commonly detected, whereas acquired antimicrobial resistance genes were infrequently detected. Genes allied with Type III and Type VI secretion systems were identified in several isolates, indicating the presence of putative virulence-associated features that require phenotypic validation. These findings provide baseline information on the identification, antimicrobial susceptibility, genomic diversity, resistance determinants, and virulence-associated genes of Aeromonas isolates recovered from diseased freshwater fish. Further studies involving larger and more geographically representative collections are needed to determine the broader epidemiological significance of these findings.

title: Facility-Type-Specific Antibiotic Use and District-Level Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Notification Patterns in Seoul: An Ecological Panel Study (2018-2024)
abstract: To describe district-level associations between antibiotic use and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) notifications in Seoul by facility type and class. In an ecological panel study of Seoul's 25 districts (2018-2024), monthly CRE notifications were linked to antibiotic claimed quantities from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service for 14 Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical level 4 classes. All models used the same district-wide CRE notification outcome, with total, acute-care hospital, clinic, or long-term care hospital quantities as exposures. Negative binomial generalized additive models included a log expected count offset and adjusted for temporal, seasonal, district-level, and covariate effects, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction within each analysis set. CRE notifications increased from 3,736 in 2018 to 10,904 in 2024, peaking at 11,218 in 2023. Positive associations were observed for 10 of 14 classes in total-use models and 11 of 14 in acute-care hospital models. Carbapenem associations were positive in total-use, acute-care hospital, and long-term care hospital models. Aminoglycoside associations were positive for total and clinic quantities. Analyses of antibiotic use by facility type identified class-specific associations with CRE notifications, which may inform setting-specific surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship.

title: A rapid, low-cost, and validated TaqMan qPCR assay for bla(KPC) surveillance in community wastewater
abstract: The rapid global dissemination of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, particularly those harboring Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (bla) genes, poses a critical threat to public health. Effective containment requires robust diagnostic tools applicable to both clinical and complex environmental matrices. We developed and validated a TaqMan-based qPCR method targeting a hyper-conserved region of blaidentified through alignment of 271 full-length sequences. Optimized at an annealing temperature of 62 °C, the assay achieved a nominal limit of detection (LOD) of 0.98 copies per reaction (estimated from genomic DNA mass), a linear quantification across nearly seven orders of magnitude (1.53 to 1 × 10copies/reaction, R > 0.99) with an amplification efficiency of 98.61%, and good repeatability (CV < 3% based on Ct values). Validation with three wastewater metagenomic samples and 33 bacterial isolates (including 5 bla-positive isolates recovered from wastewater, and 28 bla-negative bacteria), using WGS as the reference, showed perfect agreement (Kappa = 1.00). Among 50 community wastewater samples, 22.00% (11/50) were bla-positive, and culture yielded five bla-positive K. pneumoniae strains, all confirmed by whole-genome sequencing as high-risk ST15 harboring the yersiniabactin-associated virulence locus ybt14/ICEKp12, blaand bla, and porin- and quinolone-resistance-associated mutations. With a 40-min amplification time, simple operation, and a reagent cost of USD 0.13 per reaction, this method is well-suited for large-scale environmental surveillance and early warning of antimicrobial resistance dissemination.

title: Engineered Peptide Nanoparticle Targeting Both Bacterial Load Reduction and Bone Repair for the Treatment of Bone Infections
abstract: Bone infection is a common and serious complication in orthopedic surgery. Conventional antibiotic strategies frequently induce antibiotic resistance, leading to the persistence of bone infections. In this study, an engineered peptide nanoparticle named C8-IK21 was designed based on the coiled-coil motif. Specifically, C8-IK21 effectively targeted bacterial cell membranes, further exacerbating bacterial death through lipid peroxidation. At safe doses, local administration of C8-IK21 demonstrated high efficacy in treating S. aureus-infected cortical bone defects in mice. No detectable resistance emerged under the tested experimental conditions. Additionally, C8-IK21 exhibited anti-inflammatory activity. Furthermore, C8-IK21 could enter cells by binding to ADAM9, activating the ERK signaling pathway to regulate osteoblast differentiation. Meanwhile, C8-IK21 reduced the expression of ITGB1 via ADAM9, thereby inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Moreover, the pro-osteogenic effect of C8-IK21 was validated in organoids. In conclusion, C8-IK21 represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of refractory bacterial infections and bone homeostasis disorders.

title: Comparative genomic analysis of Acinetobacter baumannii strains suggests possible human risk with environmentally distributed sequence type 1
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii belongs to clinically significant opportunistic pathogens that has already been emerged as a major global health threat due to its remarkable capacity to acquire and disseminate antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Understanding the phenotypic and genotypic relationships between its clinical and environmental strains, hence is essential for tracking the dissemination of resistant strains and also for mitigating the spread of AMR. Comprehensive surveillance of clinical and environmental samples for A. baumannii is essential to identify the evolution of clinically relevant strains. In the study, detailed morphological characterization, antimicrobial susceptibility testing and biofilm formation assays were performed to screen the pathogenic strains of A. baumannii from clinical and environmental samples. Phenotypic screening conducted in the study has yielded 85 strains of A. baumannii, which included isolates from clinical (60), soil (16), and water (9) samples. Among these, 23 strains were multi-drug resistant (MDR), with 21 having clinical, and 2 with environmental origin respectively. Further to this extensively drug resistant (XDR) strain from each clinical and environmental origin was subjected to Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) analysis. Bioinformatic pipelines, including PubMLST, RAST, CARD, MGE, PHASTER, PathogenFinder, and Mauve​ were further used to predict the resistomes, mobile genetic elements, and the functional metabolite biosynthetic potential of sequenced genome. The CARD analysis has further identified clinically significant antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) such as bla, blaand lpsB genes, along with plasmids Tn6018, ISAba26 and ISAba13 that carries genes related to major antibiotic resistance and gene encoding AbaQ efflux pump in the sequenced genome. Alignment between WGS data of sequenced A. baumannii strains such as C3 and E2 has further been carried out along with the comparative phylogenomic dataset composed of global (29) and Indian (16) A. baumannii genomes retrieved from from BV-BRC. Global phylogenetic analysis has demonstrated the environmental strain E2 to come under a novel Sequence Type ST3394. This was having close alignment with a distinct clinical clade containing the high-risk international clones GC1/ ST1. The two sequenced strains have also been observed to have shared K- and O- loci as similar to other clinically relevant ST1 clade. Subsequent pangenome and Mauve analyses have further confirmed the genetic homology and minimal structural rearrangements between the selected environmental and clinical strains of A. baumannii. The observed similarities suggest a possible epidemiological relationship or shared lineage between clinical and environmental A. baumannii strains isolated in the study, which need to be further confirmed by large scale isolation, comparison and analysis.

title: Rapid carbapenemase detection in enterobacterales using a lateral flow immunoassay: diagnostic performance and association with antimicrobial treatment decisions
journal: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
abstract: Data on the association between same-day reporting of carbapenemase testing results using lateral flow immunochromatographic assays (LFA) and antimicrobial treatment decisions remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between an LFA and commercial qPCR for carbapenemase detection and to compare the LFA with the Carba NP-direct test (CNPtd) and modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM). We also assessed the association between LFA results and same-day antimicrobial treatment decisions. The study included 110 retrospective (80 carbapenemase-producing and 30 non-carbapenemase-producing) and 95 prospective Enterobacterales isolates. Agreement between the Carbapenem Resistant Enterobacteriaceae Test-Kit (Dynamiker Biotechnology, Tianjin, China), CNPtd, mCIM, and the Biospeedy Carbapenem Resistance qPCR Kit (Bioeksen, Türkiye) was evaluated using positive percent agreement (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA). The association between LFA positivity and treatment escalation was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. In the retrospective cohort, the LFA showed 100% PPA and NPA with qPCR for carbapenemase detection, whereas CNPtd and mCIM showed PPA values of 85.0% and 80.0%, respectively, with 100% NPA for both methods. In the prospective cohort, the LFA also showed 100% PPA and NPA, whereas CNPtd and mCIM showed PPA values of 74.2% and 87.1%, respectively, with 100% NPA for both methods. Complete agreement between LFA and qPCR for carbapenemase type identification was observed in 106 of 111 qPCR-positive isolates (95.5%); five discrepancies involved isolates initially identified as carrying two carbapenemase genes by qPCR. In the prospective series, 31 of 95 isolates were carbapenemase-positive by qPCR, and the LFA showed complete agreement with PCR for carbapenemase detection and type identification (31/31). Same-day treatment escalation occurred in 55.2% (16/29) of those with LFA-positive isolates, compared with 9.7% (6/62) of those with LFA-negative isolates. LFA positivity was independently associated with treatment escalation (aOR, 7.94; 95% CI, 2.44-25.83; p = 0.001). The LFA demonstrated high agreement with qPCR for both carbapenemase detection and type identification. In the prospective series, LFA positivity was associated with same-day antimicrobial treatment escalation.

title: Prevalence, genotypic characterization, and antimicrobial resistance of poultry-associated Salmonella isolates across four geographical zones of West Bengal, India
abstract: Salmonella contamination of poultry is a critical food safety and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) concern at the human-animal-environment interface. This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence, serovar distribution, multidrug resistance (MDR) profiles, genotypic resistance determinants, and biofilm-forming capacity from commercial slaughter poultry across four zones of West Bengal, India. A total of 300 biological samples (faecal, caecal, meat; 25 per sample type per zone) were collected from 20 slaughterhouses across Burdwan, Midnapore, Nadia, and South 24 Parganas. Culture-based prevalence was 32.7% (98/300; 95% CI: 27.6-38.2%); significant zone-wise heterogeneity was observed (χ² = 13.64, df = 3, p = 0.003), with Nadia recording the highest prevalence (46.7%). No significant sample-type effect was detected (p = 0.192), consistent with systemic gut-to-carcass contamination. Of the 98 culture-based presumptive Salmonella isolates, 37 were confirmed as Salmonella by invA and serovar-specific gene amplification, among which 21.6% were identified as S. Typhimurium, 24.3% as S. Enteritidis, and 54.1% remained untypable. Antibiotic susceptibility testing revealed universal resistance to amoxicillin-clavulanate and doxycycline; co-trimoxazole resistance was 86.5%, neomycin 75.7%, levofloxacin 43.2%, and enrofloxacin 40.5%; MDR was present in 91.9% (34/37). Sanger sequencing of gyrA QRDR from 20 field isolates confirmed Asp87Tyr (n = 1) and Ser83Leu (n = 2); qnrS and sul1 were identified in 5 and 3 isolates, respectively. Biofilm formation was present in 91.9% (strong 21.6%, moderate 51.4%, weak 16.2%; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.518). These findings reveal an alarming convergence of high Salmonella prevalence, MDR, and WHO-critically important antimicrobial resistance in West Bengal slaughter poultry, with direct implications for food safety and One Health AMR surveillance.

title: Outcomes of ESBL status among UTI admissions: a retrospective analysis of the Nationwide Inpatient Sample from 2016 to 2022
abstract: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing organisms are an increasing cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and pose significant challenges to inpatient management due to antimicrobial resistance and limited treatment options. Prior studies focus on prevalence and resistance patterns, but nationally representative inpatient outcome data are lacking. This study assesses the association of ESBL status on clinical outcomes among hospitalized adults with UTIs in the United States. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2016 to 2022. Adult patients aged ≥ 18 years hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of UTI were included. ESBL status was identified using ICD-10-CM code Z16.12, with non-ESBL UTIs serving as the comparison group. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, while secondary outcomes included hospital length of stay (LOS) and total inflation-adjusted hospital costs. Propensity score stratification and multivariable regression adjusted for demographic, clinical, and hospital confounders. Among 1,844,239 UTI hospitalizations from 2016 to 2022, 63,190 (3.4%) involved ESBL-producing organisms. ESBL status was not associated with increased in-hospital mortality compared with non-ESBL UTIs. However, ESBL infections were associated with longer hospital stays (mean difference 1.0 days; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.10; p < 0.001) and higher total hospital charges (mean difference $9,179; 95% CI $8,101 to $10,257; p < 0.001). In this nationally representative analysis, ESBL-producing UTIs were associated with increased healthcare utilization but not higher in-hospital mortality. These findings highlight the clinical and economic burden of ESBL infections and the importance of targeted prevention and optimized inpatient management strategies.

title: Geographic distribution, genetic diversity, and virulence determinants of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli: a descriptive review of the retrieved literature
abstract: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) is an important foodborne pathogen associated with a wide range of clinical manifestations, from mild gastroenteritis to severe disease. This study aimed to synthesize the evidence retrieved on the reported occurrence and geographic distribution of STEC across different matrices, as well as their genetic diversity, virulence determinants, clinical manifestations, and antimicrobial resistance profiles. A descriptive, non-exhaustive review was conducted based on studies published between 2010 and 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 55 articles after application of the eligibility criteria. The included studies originated from different geographic regions, although the evidence was markedly concentrated in the Americas, particularly Brazil. STEC was investigated across human, animal, food, and environmental sources. Within the retrieved literature, stx2 and stx1 were widely reported, and stx2a, stx2c, and stx2d were among the recurrently reported stx2 subtypes. O157 and non-O157 STEC were both represented across the included studies. These findings describe reporting patterns within the retrieved literature and should not be interpreted as frequencies of occurrence among studies specifically testing each characteristic or as prevalence among STEC isolates. The included studies also reported diverse sequence types and additional virulence determinants, including eae and ehxA. Clinical information was available in only a subset of studies and included manifestations ranging from diarrhea and bloody diarrhea to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Antimicrobial resistance was investigated in a subset of the included studies using phenotypic and/or genotypic approaches. Resistance phenotypes and resistance-associated genetic determinants were reported among STEC isolates in different study populations; however, heterogeneity in analytical populations, antimicrobial panels, testing methods, and reporting approaches precluded overall or pooled estimates of antimicrobial resistance. Overall, the findings highlight the diversity of STEC reported across different sources and geographic settings and reinforce the importance of integrated molecular and epidemiological approaches within a One Health framework.

title: An integrated molecular, phenotypic, and adaptive analysis of polymyxin resistance in KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Rising resistance to polymyxins poses a critical challenge in the management of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Klebsiella pneumoniae. This study investigated 50 polymyxin-resistant K. pneumoniae isolates recovered from hospitals in Brazil using an integrated approach combining antimicrobial susceptibility testing, targeted molecular analysis, lipid A profiling, and phenotypic assays. Eighteen isolates were classified as XDR and 32 as MDR. All isolates carried bla, 56% co-harbored blagenes, and 62% were resistant to ceftazidime-avibactam. Targeted sequencing revealed diverse alterations in polymyxin resistance-associated loci, particularly mgrB, pmrAB, phoQ, and crrB, including amino acid substitutions, premature stop codons, insertions, and deletions. Lipid A analysis by MALDI-TOF MS confirmed structural remodeling, such as the incorporation of 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose (L-Ara4N) and phosphoethanolamine, consistent with polymyxin-resistant phenotypes. Virulence assessment using the Galleria mellonella model showed marked heterogeneity among isolates, with no direct association between resistance-associated alterations and virulence phenotypes. Short-term survival following polymyxin B exposure at pH 5.8 and 7.7 differed in only a subset of isolates, indicating a strain-dependent response to environmental conditions. In addition, the laboratory-evolved Escherichia coli D12 mutant exhibited lipid A remodeling and alterations in PmrAB following polymyxin selective pressure. Overall, these findings support the multifactorial nature of polymyxin resistance and highlight the value of integrating molecular, structural, and phenotypic approaches for antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Wetland microbiomes: diversity, biogeochemical functions, climate feedbacks, and emerging frontiers
abstract: Wetlands occupy roughly 6% of the Earth's surface yet store 20 to 30% of global soil carbon and emit an estimated 145 to 180 Tg of methane each year, fluxes that are controlled by microbial communities. This review synthesizes the past decade of research on wetland microbiomes across peatlands, mangroves, salt marshes, and constructed wetlands, and draws three main conclusions. First, community assembly is governed mainly by environmental filtering: salinity and pH are the strongest predictors, deterministic processes dominate steep gradients, and stochastic processes become important in hydrologically homogeneous settings. Second, the evidence linking microbial communities to biogeochemical fluxes is uneven in strength. Process-level measurements and meta-analyses support a well-constrained picture of methanogenesis, methane oxidation, and sulfate suppression of methanogenesis, whereas much of the evidence for cryptic sulfur cycling, anaerobic methane oxidation coupled to nitrogen species, and viral regulation rests on gene abundance, which reports functional potential rather than in situ activity. Third, in constructed wetlands, antibiotic removal does not necessarily reduce antimicrobial resistance risks, because antibiotic concentrations, resistance gene abundance, mobile genetic elements, and horizontal gene transfer respond to different environmental drivers. The most pressing unresolved questions are the controls on the N₂O: N₂ product ratio of denitrification, the scaling from gene abundance to ecosystem fluxes, and the joint response of greenhouse-gas emissions to interacting climate drivers. We close by identifying where multi-omics integration and standardized cross-site observation networks would most rapidly close these gaps.

title: pH-Responsive Delivery of D-Amino Acids by Pillar[5]arene for Enhanced Antibiofilm and Antibacterial Activities
abstract: Biofilms are a promising target to combat antibiotic resistance, but D-amino acids require high doses for biofilm inhibition. To overcome this, a novel antibiofilm agent was designed by anchoring D-amino acids onto the pillar[5]arene scaffold via acid-labile imine linkages. Pillar[5]arenes functionalized with D-amino acids showed enhanced antibiofilm activities compared to free D-amino acids, attributed to the localized release of D-amino acids within biofilms. Moreover, synergy was observed when conventional antibiotics ERY and TET were combined with PAY10. Benefiting from biofilm disruption, the combined treatment exposed bacteria to antibiotics, thereby improving MRSA susceptibility. In addition, the pillar[5]arene derivatives exhibited no cytotoxicity at the tested concentrations. Lastly, the expression levels of AgrA and dltD genes in MRSA were downregulated after treatment with PAY10. This revealed that the compound reduced biofilm mass by quenching quorum-sensing signals and repressing the production of extracellular polymeric substances.

title: A core genome multilocus sequence typing scheme for Bacteroides fragilis: insights into population structure and genomic epidemiology
abstract: strains are important members of the human gut microbiota and represent major opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of anaerobic infections. Their clinical relevance is reinforced by diverse antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and a complex population structure comprising two major phylogenetic lineages, Division I and Division II. Although whole-genome sequencing is increasingly used for bacterial surveillance, no standardized core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme is available for, limiting high-resolution and comparable genomic analyses. In this study, we developed a cgMLST scheme comprising 2,342 highly conserved loci applicable across both Divisions. The scheme was developed from 433 publicly available genomes with diverse geographic origins, sample types, and isolation periods. It was subsequently evaluated using 118 newly sequenced infection-associated isolates from France not included in scheme development. Clustering analysis identified an accurate single-linkage threshold of 400 allelic mismatches, providing balanced resolution for population structure analyses and high concordance with core genome phylogeny and classical MLST sequence types. Well-defined clusters were identified within both Divisions, with genetic profiles indicative of long-standing evolutionary divergence. These clusters showed no clear association with geographic origin, isolation source, or sampling period. Notably, some clusters were enriched in-positive and multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates, including one in particular that emerged as a genetically divergent MDR-associated lineage within Division II. This cgMLST scheme provides a standardized and high-resolution framework forgenotyping. Its implementation in the publicly accessible BIGSdb-Pasteur platform (https://bigsdb.pasteur.fr/) will support global genomic surveillance and future epidemiological studies. strains hold a position of relevance within the human gut microbiota, as they represent a major cause of severe anaerobic infections. Defining genotypes is essential for tracking infections and monitoring the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance. In this study, we developed a core genome multilocus sequence typing scheme forand applied it to a large collection of isolates from diverse origins. Our results reveal a structured population with well-defined and genetically conserved clusters across both Divisions, consistent with a long-standing population structure. Notably, several clusters were enriched in antimicrobial resistance determinants and multidrug-resistant isolates. This study also provides an easy-to-use resource for global surveillance and future epidemiological investigations of this clinically important pathogen.

title: Evaluating facility-level variability in urinary antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in long-term care homes in Ontario, Canada
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance surveillance in long-term care homes is limited by its reliance on organism-specific summaries, most commonly, which may not reflect the broader microbiological landscape in these settings. We evaluated how-based urinary susceptibility compared with weighted-incidence syndromic combination antibiograms (WISCA), a composite measure incorporating multiple pathogens, across 627 Ontario long-term care homes in 2023. Facility-level antimicrobial susceptibilities to eight antibiotics were estimated using 23,750 urinary isolates, with missing data addressed through imputation, and estimates stabilized using random-intercept logistic regression models.accounted for a mean of 50.6% (standard deviation = 1.9) of urinary isolates, with the remaining 49.5% mainly comprising(16.6% [0.8]),(11.9% [1.2]),(6.6% [2.1]), and(6.1% [0.1]). Organism-specific susceptibility varied substantially across antibiotics, particularly for ciprofloxacin susceptibility in(78.7% [13.1]) and(48.9% [11.5]), and nitrofurantoin susceptibility in(48.5% [9.0]). Compared with-based estimates, WISCA susceptibilities were lower for seven of eight antibiotics, most notably for nitrofurantoin (WISCA: 70.6% vs96.8%). These findings suggest that reliance onalone may not fully capture facility-level urinary susceptibility patterns, as variation in pathogen distribution and organism-specific antibiotic susceptibilities across homes can produce substantially different susceptibility estimates. WISCA provides a more representative and stable measure by incorporating pathogen diversity and weighting organism prevalence. Integrating this into antimicrobial resistance surveillance for long-term care homes may improve the detection of emerging resistance trends and better inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies by identifying variable organism-antibiotic combinations.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial resistance is a growing concern in long-term care homes, where infections are common, and antibiotics are frequently used. Surveillance in these settings often relies onto estimate how well antibiotics will work, but this approach may not capture the range of urinary pathogens encountered in these settings, differences in resistance between organisms, or how these differences can vary across long-term care homes. In this study,represented only about half of the urinary infections, while other organisms includinganddemonstrated differing susceptibility levels across antibiotics. These findings support the value of organism-inclusive surveillance, such as weighted-incidence syndromic combination antibiograms, to provide a more comprehensive picture of resistance and better inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies in long-term care homes.

title: One Health, no silos: integrating veterinary, human, and environmental stewardship strategies to close the AMR diagnostic gap in the United States
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global crisis that threatens the health of humans, animals, and the environment. It has been projected that if not urgently and judiciously addressed, there could be up to 10 million deaths each year by 2050 caused by AMR infections. AMR is not a static or easily eradicated issue tied to a singular source; it emerges from intersecting pressures across human, animal, and environmental health and is exacerbated by the misuse and potential excessive use of antimicrobials. This review highlights the importance of an integrated, One-Health approach in tackling AMR, underscoring the need for a coordinated antimicrobial stewardship process that centers on optimal diagnostic approaches spanning all sectors. Significant gaps in diagnostics persist between human and veterinary medicine, especially with regard to diagnostic capacity, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and standardized reporting. In environmental settings, additional challenges include suboptimal effluent and waste management, continued reliance on antimicrobials for non-therapeutic purposes, and inconsistent soil and water management practices. Taken together, these issues hinder the ability to manage AMR, while the siloed nature of these three primary sectors complicates data integration and ultimately weakens global surveillance and mitigation efforts. To improve One Health antimicrobial stewardship strategies, we must strengthen diagnostic capacity, harmonize antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) methods across human and veterinary health, and integrate surveillance systems to include environmental sources worldwide. Further development and investment in rapid diagnostics, standardized protocols, and collaborative data-sharing frameworks is crucial in addressing local and global AMR to ensure the effectiveness of antimicrobials for future generations.

title: Complete genome sequences of nine novel Enterococcus species recovered from dairy, swine, and imported foods in Canada
abstract: Studying antimicrobial resistance transmission in Canadian agroecosystems, we isolated nine new species offrom dairy farms in British Columbia and Quebec and one swine farm in Quebec, as well as from food imported to Canada. Here, we report the complete genome sequences of ten isolates representing nine novel species.

title: In vitro efficacy of synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33 against poultry isolates with diverse antimicrobial resistance phenotypes
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an impactful One Health issue. One of its drivers is the extensive use of antibiotics in both human and animal production systems, and despite regulatory restrictions on antibiotic use in poultry farming, antimicrobial resistance remains a major challenge. Consequently, animals are at higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs, highlighting the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. Toward this end, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum activity and lower propensity to induce resistance. However, the effectiveness of AMPs against poultry pathogens, and in particular multidrug-resistant strains, is largely unclear. Here, we evaluated SET-M33, a synthetic tetrabranched AMP, against four species of clinically relevant pathogens in poultry, namely,,,, and. Using a panel of 141 field isolates, we found that SET-M33 broadly inhibited bacterial growth at low micromolar concentrations (median minimum inhibitory concentrations of 2.5 and 5 μM for gram-negative and gram-positive strains, respectively), including in multidrug-resistant isolates. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on host cells, we established anco-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability. These findings demonstrate the potential of SET-M33 as a new antimicrobial agent against pathogens in poultry. Antimicrobial resistance is an important One Health issue that affects human and animal health. In particular, antimicrobial resistance remains a challenge in poultry farming, where animals are at a higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs. To solve this issue, we need alternative antimicrobial strategies, and antimicrobial peptides have emerged as particularly promising candidates. Here, we examined the efficacy of one such new antimicrobial, the synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33, against a large panel of poultry pathogen isolates. We found that SET-M33 was highly effective against the vast majority of isolates, including strains that are multidrug resistant or resistant to other antimicrobial peptides. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on the host, we established anco-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability.

title: A dual-action combination therapy targeting bacteria and host immunity against bacterial infections
abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, coupled with a stagnant novel antibiotic discovery pipeline, underscores the urgent need for innovative strategies to combat bacterial infections. The development of antibiotic adjuvants that increase the efficacy of existing drugs represents a critical approach for addressing this challenge. We demonstrate that combining the conventional antibiotic azithromycin with the quorum-sensing inhibitor norharmane exerts potent antibacterial effects through both direct bactericidal activity and host immune activation. This combination not only disrupts bacterial structural integrity but also promotes macrophage polarization toward the M1-type phenotype and upregulates the expression of the important mediator, Muc5b, through activation of the IL-17 signaling pathway, ultimately enhancing mucosal immune defense and tissue repair functions. This regimen shows potent antibacterial efficacy against a range of pathogensand, along with a favorable safety profile. These findings highlight a promising combinatorial therapeutic strategy against the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotic resistance has become one of the most urgent threats to global public health, yet the development of new antibiotics has slowed dramatically. In this study, we propose a promising alternative strategy that combines azithromycin with a small-molecule compound capable of inhibiting bacterial quorum sensing. This combination not only kills bacteria more effectively than the antibiotic alone but also harnesses the body's own immune system to fight infection. Its mechanisms of action include disrupting bacterial structure, promoting the polarization of macrophages toward the M1-type phenotype, and enhancing bactericidal capacity by activating the IL-17 signaling pathway to stimulate the production of the Muc5b protein. Our findings suggest that this dual-pronged approach could help revitalize existing antibiotics, offering a practical pathway to combat drug-resistant infections.

title: Genomic characterization of a Brazilian multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 isolate associated with bovine mastitis
abstract: This study presents the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (MDR-Kp) isolate (LC808) obtained from a case of bovine mastitis in Brazil. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed an MDR phenotype, indicating resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The presence of an extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) was also confirmed. Whole-genome sequencing identified the isolate as sequence type 17 (ST17) and revealed the presence of the KL127 and O13 loci. The resistome contained genes associated with antimicrobial resistance, including bla, bla, bla, and bla(β-lactams); aph(6)-Id, aph(3'')-Ib, aph(3')-Ia, aac(3)-IIe, and aac(6')-Ib10 (aminoglycosides); tet(A) (tetracyclines); qnrB17 (fluoroquinolones); and sul2 (sulfonamides). A class 1 integron carrying dfrA14 was also identified. The virulome included type 1 and type 3 fimbriae, a type VI secretion system, and multiple iron-acquisition systems (fecABCDEIR). Identifying this clinically relevant lineage that carries multiple resistance and virulence determinants highlights the presence of MDR-Kp in bovine mastitis in Brazil. These findings provide the necessary genomic baseline data to support ongoing genomic surveillance of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in dairy herds within a One Health framework.

title: Gram-negative antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in wild and captive birds: a narrative review of ecological niches and One Health implications
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in birds is increasingly investigated because wild and captive birds can encounter resistant bacteria at interfaces involving human activity, other animals, and environmental contamination. This narrative review synthesizes reports of antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in wild, captive, and other non-poultry avian populations. Rather than treating all detections as equivalent, the evidence is interpreted across distinct levels: bacterial occurrence or carriage, phenotypic resistance, antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), bacterial lineage relatedness, and epidemiological or experimentally demonstrated transmission. The literature shows recurrent detection of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, blagenes, multidrug-resistant phenotypes, and diverse ARGs across multiple ecological settings. However, substantial heterogeneity in sampling, bacterial recovery, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and molecular characterization limits direct comparison among studies and restricts inference regarding persistence, dissemination, and transmission. The central contribution of this review is therefore an ecological and molecular evidence framework that distinguishes exposure and carriage from persistence, genetic mobility, genomic relatedness, and transmission. The review also identifies methodological priorities, including harmonized sampling and susceptibility testing, longitudinal studies, cross-compartment sampling, genomic characterization, and explicit integration of ecological and epidemiological data.

title: Unveiling novel therapeutic targets and potent hits to combat antimicrobial resistance in Bacteroides fragilis
abstract: The opportunistic anaerobic bacterium Bacteroides fragilis is an important human pathogen associated with a variety of infections, including intra-abdominal abscesses, peritonitis, bacteremia, lung abscesses and surgical site infections. The growing number of strains that are multidrug-resistant (MDR) in B. fragilis has raised attention to identify new therapeutic targets and discover potent antimicrobial drugs. An integrative computational approach was used in this study to highlight promising inhibitors against B. fragilis and identify potential therapeutic targets. The present study identified 18 essential proteins from the B. fragilis proteome that contribute to virulence and pathogenicity and play critical roles in bacterial survival. Furthermore, protein-protein interactions (PPI's) network analysis, functional annotation, and enrichment analyses identified tetraacyldisaccharide 4'-kinase (LpxK) as the most promising druggable target, owing to its essential role in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis in Gram-negative bacteria. Structure-guided drug design identified five high-affinity LpxK inhibitors. DFT and molecular dynamics analyses confirmed stable binding and conformational stability. Furthermore, these findings provide a theoretical basis for the rational development of targeted antibacterial agents against multidrug-resistant B. fragilis towards infectious disease control, and lay the foundation for future experimental evaluation and optimization.

title: Aptamer-Based Fluorescent Assays for Detection of the Host-Response Viral Biomarker 3'-Deoxy-3',4'-Didehydro-Cytidine
abstract: Improved viral diagnostics are urgently needed to strengthen pandemic preparedness and combat antimicrobial resistance, highlighting the importance of 3'-deoxy-3',4'-didehydro-cytidine (ddhC), a host-derived, pan-viral biomarker that addresses key limitations of PCR-based diagnostics. Current methods for ddhC measurement rely on liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) or nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which are accurate but costly and impractical for rapid or point-of-care testing. Here, we report the development of aptamer-based fluorescent assays for selective ddhC detection. Low-micromolar-affinity DNA aptamers were isolated using capture-systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) and characterised by isothermal titration calorimetry. Using a common core aptamer sequence, three fluorescence assay formats-strand displacement, molecular beacon, and dye displacement-were developed and evaluated. Independent LC-MS analysis demonstrated a strong correlation between creatinine-normalised urinary and serum ddhC concentrations in inpatient samples (R = 0.98, p <0.0001), supporting urine as a non-invasive matrix for ddhC detection. Among the three aptamer-based formats tested, the dye displacement assay exhibited the lowest functional Kd but was limited in urine by inner filter effects, whereas a Cy5-labelled strand displacement assay overcame this limitation and detected ddhC in patient urine with moderate correlation to LC-MS (R = 0.76, p = 0.001). Together, these results establish aptamer-based sensing approaches for ddhC and demonstrate their feasibility in clinical urine samples, providing a foundation for further optimisation toward accessible, non-invasive, and rapid detection of acute viral infection.

title: Fate and effects of emerging contaminants during anaerobic digestion of organic wastes: Effective exposure, mechanisms and intervention strategies
abstract: Methane recovery from anaerobic digestion can be held back by emerging contaminants, and so can the range of uses open to the digestate. This review covers pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, micro- and nanoplastics, and selected engineered nanomaterials in sludge, manure, food waste, and industrial residues. The synthesis draws on comparisons within individual studies to examine how contaminant form, contact with biomass, and exposure duration shape responses at individual steps of anaerobic digestion. Reversals between stimulation and inhibition appear in dose series for perfluorobutanesulfonate and for bisphenol A. Inhibition can also emerge once exposure is prolonged, at a point that short-term tests do not reach. Among the interventions examined, gains in methane recovery do not necessarily coincide with gains in contaminant transformation or in antibiotic-resistance outcomes. Two separate tasks are involved: restoring inhibited digestion, and improving contaminant transformation without losing methane production. Products left behind by transformation can retain biological activity. Phase-resolved mass balances are a way to tell genuine destruction apart from transfer into concentrates and spent media. Engineering comparisons show that a benefit can fade even when the material is still in place, and that a higher electrical input can return less additional methane. Intervention selection should account for the limiting conversion step, the residues relevant to the intended use of digestate, and the energy, materials and maintenance needed to sustain treatment.

title: [Public Health as an Elective in the Final Clinical Year in Baden-Württemberg, Germany: Results of a Mixed-Methods Study on Elective Evaluation and Development of an Evaluation Instrument]
abstract: In light of global challenges such as pandemics, social inequality, antibiotic resistance, and climate change, public health perspectives are becoming increasingly important in medical care. However, medical education remains predominantly focused on individual patient care. Content related to public health and practical insights into public health services (PHS) have so far been incorporated into the curriculum only to a limited extent. Since November 2023, it has been possible to take a public health elective at six pilot teaching local public health authorities (LHA) in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the implementation of this public health elective. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, qualitative individual interviews were conducted with students and supervisors from six pilot LHA. Based on these findings, a questionnaire instrument for the long-term evaluation of the public health elective was developed and piloted. Five students and five staff members from LHA were interviewed. Eight of the 14 students participated in the survey. The public health elective was rated positively overall by both students and supervisors. The students surveyed highlighted the structured orientation, the dedicated supervision, and the flexibility in rotation planning and working hours. All students reported gaining a good overview of LHA activities. Six out of eight students gave the highest grade, and all will recommend it to others. Practical competencies were acquired primarily in the Child and Adolescent Health Service, the HIV/STI service, and in infection control. Criticisms included the logbook, which was perceived as too extensive and not very practice-oriented, as well as the cross-site organization of the public health elective support classes. The results suggest that the public health elective can help raise awareness of PHS and help medical students with their career planning. Given the global challenges, the public health elective can help incorporate public health perspectives into medical education and provide hands-on experience in this field. Furthermore, there are indications that the introduction of the public health elective may also stimulate organizational development within LHA. Due to the small sample size and potential selection bias, generalizability of findings is limited.

title: Genomic epidemiology and transmission dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii: Comparison of clinical and wastewater isolates
abstract: This study characterized the epidemiological, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii across inpatient, outpatient, hospital environmental, and diverse wastewater habitats from January to December 2025. Bacterial detection exhibited pronounced seasonal variations and habitat heterogeneity, with wastewater showing the highest prevalence and summer marking the peak period. High-touch surfaces represented the core hospital contamination nodes, and healthcare workers faced potential risks of carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) colonization. Notably, CRAB and multidrug-resistant strains appeared confined to clinical niches, where the dominant ST2and ST164clones stably harbored abundant carbapenemases, disinfectant resistance genes, and virulence factors. Anthropogenic antibiotic and sanitizer selective pressures likely drive their high multiple antibiotic resistance index (MARI) phenotypes. Conversely, wastewater strains were predominantly pan-susceptible (MARI < 0.2) but enriched with novel sequence types (STs) and rare resistance genes, suggesting their role as a natural reservoir for genetic diversification. Core-genome SNP transmission networks indicated high-density intra-hospital cross-transmission and occult inter-hospital dissemination, while capturing potential bidirectional cross-habitat spillover events. Mechanistically, conjugative plasmids, insertion sequences (IS256/IS3/IS66), and active prophages mediated resistance and virulence recombination in clinical strains. Meanwhile, wastewater strains might utilize the ISNCY family to undergo environmental adaptation, with integrons playing a minor role in resistance spread. This study uncovers the divergent evolutionary pathways of A. baumannii, providing critical genomic evidence for integrated clinical-environmental management to mitigate the cross-niche dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Acquired antimicrobial resistance in clinical and hospital-environment isolates in onco-haematology: Detection of blaVIM-4/blaPER-1 in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and aac(6')-Ib-cr/sul2/dfrA1 in Burkholderia cepacia
abstract: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and Burkholderia cepacia are opportunistic saprophytic bacteria that have emerged as important pathogens in immunocompromised patients. The objective of this study was to characterize antimicrobial resistance determinants in clinical and environmental isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia and to assess their potential clinical relevance. A total of 71 clinical isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia, collected between 2018 and 2022, and 25 environmental isolates collected in 2023, were identified using the Analytical Profile Index 20NE (API 20NE). Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by the disc diffusion method and the Epsilometer test (E-test). The double-disc synergy test screened for extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) activity; resistance genes were detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the genetic context of blaVIM-4 was investigated by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 51 S. maltophilia and 12 B. cepacia strains were resistant to at least one antibiotic. An ESBL phenotype was detected in 34 S. maltophilia and six B. cepacia strains. We report the detection of blaVIM-4 and blaPER-1 in S. maltophilia, and of aac(6')-Ib-cr, sul2, and dfrA1 in B. cepacia. Genomic analysis suggested a probable chromosomal location of blaVIM-4 within a class 1 integron, alongside aac(6')-II, dfrA1, and sul1, flanked by TnpR- and TnpA-family transposases, in an ST78 S. maltophilia strain. Although the S. maltophilia species is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems, the detection of blaVIM-4 highlights the importance of further investigation to study the potential mobilization and horizontal transfer of this gene to susceptible species in clinical settings.

title: Evaluation of antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity and molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran
abstract: P. aeruginosa is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections and is recognized by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen due to its intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms and its remarkable capacity for biofilm formation. This study aimed to evaluate antibiotic resistance profiles, biofilm formation capacity, and the molecular detection of resistance genes in clinical P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from hospitalized patients in Ilam, Iran. A total of 44 non-duplicate P. aeruginosa isolates were collected from urine, blood, and sputum specimens between November 2023 and August 2024. Identification used standard microbiological and biochemical tests. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion following CLSI guidelines, and colistin MIC was determined by broth microdilution. Biofilm formation was assessed using a microtiter plate assay with crystal violet staining. Major resistance genes, including β-lactamases (-GES,-CTX,-SHV,-TEM), metallo-β-lactamases (-NDM,-VIM,-IMP), and fluoroquinolone resistance determinants (parC, parE), were detected via PCR. The isolates exhibited high resistance rates to aztreonam (100%), gentamicin (68.2%), and imipenem (59.1%), while amikacin remained the most effective agent (95.5% susceptible). Following broth microdilution, colistin resistance was only 2.3%. Molecular analysis revealed that-GES (100%) and parC (95.5%) were the most prevalent resistance genes. followed by-CTX (55.5%),-SHV (45.5%),-TEM (45.5%), parE (36.4%),-NDM (13.6%),-VIM (13.6%), and-IMP (4.5%). Biofilm formation was observed in all isolates: 68.2% weak, 31.8% moderate; no strong producers were identified. A significant association was found between anatomical specimen source and biofilm strength (p = 0.011), with sputum isolates showing the highest moderate biofilm formation (75%). However, no significant association was observed between biofilm phenotype and antibiotic resistance. The coexistence of MDR-associated genes and biofilm-forming ability underscores P. aeruginosa as a critical MDR pathogen. The high prevalence ofGES and parC, combined with the association between respiratory origin and moderate biofilm formation, highlights its adaptive success. Continuous surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, routine colistin MIC testing, and anti-biofilm therapeutic approaches are essential to mitigate the clinical impact of MDR P. aeruginosa infections.

title: Detection of blaVIM, blaIMP, blaNDM, blaKPC and blaOXA-48-like carbapenemase genes in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales clinical isolates with phenotypic and genotypic antimicrobial susceptibility to colistin
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are WHO critical-priority pathogens, and detection of carbapenemase production and mcr-1-mediated colistin resistance is important for guiding therapy and preventing antimicrobial resistance spread. In this prospective cross-sectional study, a total of 144 non-duplicate CRE clinical isolates were subjected to the Modified Carbapenem Inactivation Method (mCIM) ± EDTA-modified Carbapenem Inactivation Method (eCIM) test, followed by in-house (laboratory-developed) conventional multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for simultaneous detection of five common carbapenemase genes, viz. blaVIM, blaIMP, blaNDM, blaKPC and blaOXA-48-like genes. Colistin susceptibility was performed by the broth microdilution method, followed by in-house (laboratory-developed) conventional PCR to detect mcr-1 gene. 73.6% (106/144) of CRE isolates were positive for mCIM test, i.e., CP-CRE, while 96% (102/106) of them were positive for eCIM test. Among eCIM positive CRE (i.e., Metallo-β-lactamase producers), 56% (57/102) were positive for blaNDM gene, 9.8% (10/102) were positive for blaVIM gene, and 2.9% (3/102) were positive for blaIMP gene. Among eCIM negative mCIM positive CRE (i.e., Serine ± Metallo-β-lactamase producers), all four were positive for blaOXA-48-like gene. Colistin had intermediate susceptibility of 90.3% (130/144). mcr-1 gene was detected in five isolates i.e., three with colistin resistant isolates (21.4%; 3/14) and two in colistin intermediate cases with MIC 1 and 2 µg/mL each. Majority of CRE in Indian settings were CP-CRE, with predominance of Metallo-β-lactamase producers (MBL-CRE). blaNDM gene was the most common carbapenemase gene. Colistin resistance (9.7%) was spreading fast, with the mcr-1 gene (21.4%) being a significant contributor.

title: Stage-Resolved Dynamics of Antibiotic Resistance Genes and Mobile Genetic Elements in Full-Scale Anaerobic Digestion Systems
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) has the potential to reduce antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) during waste treatment, yet evidence from full-scale systems remains limited. In particular, process-stage dynamics and host-associated resistance mechanisms are poorly understood, and the relative importance of operational and physicochemical drivers remains unresolved. Here, we profiled process-oriented, stage-resolved resistome and mobilome dynamics across substrates, digestates, and storages from ten farm-scale AD plants, resolving putative host-ARG-MGE coabundance associations across sequential process stages. An integrated framework combining high-throughput qPCR and 16S rRNA gene sequencing was used to quantify ARG and MGE dynamics and characterize microbial community structure. Across different AD systems, ARGs and MGEs exhibited heterogeneous abundance changes, with no consistent patterns. However, elevated pH and NH3 were associated with decreasing trends but were not solely determinative. Stage-resolved correlation networks revealed that ARG-MGE associations formed a conserved structural backbone, whereas putative host associations underwent continuous reshuffling across process stages. This indicates that resistance persistence is driven less by stable taxon associations and more by the redistribution of ARG-MGE units among microbial taxa. Collectively, these results demonstrate that stage-resolved, network-informed analyses provide an informative framework for evaluating resistance persistence and potential environmental risks associated with digestate application.

title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure
abstract: Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled 'safe period' of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.

title: Phage-Based Biofilm Control in Engineered Water Environments
abstract: Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.

title: Outer Membrane Vesicles as a Potential Pathway for Antibiotic Resistance Transfer between Cyanobacteria and Bacteria
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have profoundly exacerbated environmental risks to public health, evolving into a pressing ecological dilemma. Distinct from traditional pathways, outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are emerging as important vectors for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in aquatic environments, yet their role in inter-phylum ARG dissemination remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that OMVs mediate bidirectional HGT of ARGs between the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and Escherichia coli DH5α. Co-incubation experiments confirmed that OMVs derived from either strain could associate with the other, accompanied by successful functional expression of transferred resistance genes. In simulated aquatic environmental conditions, OMVs supplementation increased HGT frequency by 1.49-2.27 folds compared to the control group on day 5. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that OMVs carrying resistance genes induced subtle shifts in coastal microbial community composition. Our findings establish OMVs as mobile genetic packages that enable ARGs exchange between cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria, highlighting a previously overlooked pathway for environmental dissemination of ARGs and providing a theoretical basis for mitigating antibiotic resistance risks in aquatic ecosystems.

title: One Health phylogenomics of antibiotic-resistant Salmonella enterica reveals cross-source relatedness and detection of mcr-3-carrying ST34 isolates in Hong Kong
abstract: Nontyphoidalserovars are a major driver of foodborne illnesses in Hong Kong. Beyond well-recognized extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)- and carbapenemase-producing strains, colistin resistance remains a critical concern for treating severe multidrug-resistant (MDR) infections. While routine surveillance exists, the distribution and genomic epidemiology of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across interconnected reservoirs remain insufficiently characterized. Applying a One Health framework, this study investigated cross-sectoral genetic relatedness and shared AMR determinants by analyzing local clinical and retail meatisolates alongside a reference set of publicly available regional genomes representing human, food, animal, and environmental sectors. We report the detection of-positive. Typhimurium ST34 lineage human clinical isolates in Hong Kong, includingand, not previously detected in our regional dataset or local genomic surveillance archives. Nanopore sequencing revealed thatwas carried on a mosaic IncC/IncFII plasmid displaying structural features consistent with a recombinant origin involving genetic elements shared between clinicaland chicken-derivedplasmid backbones. These plasmids demonstrated hightransferability to diverse Enterobacterales, including,andspp. Additionally, identification of a transferable--carrying plasmid from a pork-derived isolate highlights the presence andmobility of clinically important carbapenenemase determinants within food-derived strains. Comparative phylogenomic analysis of 1,458genomes identified mixed-source genomic clusters among major sequence types (ST19, ST34, ST155, ST40, ST17, and ST2529), indicating genomic relatedness across multiple One Health sectors. These findings support the utility of integrated One Health genomic surveillance frameworks to monitor multidrug-resistantlineages.

title: Soil antibiotic resistance genes at the One Health interface: Evidence trajectories, dissemination risks, and risk-based management
abstract: Soils serve as reservoirs and transmission interfaces for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which can function as mobile genetic contaminants by persisting and replicating within microbial hosts and propagating via horizontal gene transfer (HGT). However, evidence linking mitigation mechanisms to environmental risk reduction remains insufficiently synthesized. Here, we integrate bibliometric trajectory analysis with mechanistic synthesis, using 2,309 Web of Science Core Collection records published between 2008 and 2026 to identify research trajectories, knowledge structures, and emerging mitigation fronts. The field has shifted from occurrence surveys and source identification toward intervention-oriented control, accelerating markedly after 2019. Foundational knowledge centers on soil resistome dynamics, mobile genetic element (MGE)-mediated HGT, and contaminant-driven co-selection. Current fronts highlight biochar-mediated regulation, manure and compost management, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-driven or photocatalytic inactivation of extracellular deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and ARG responses under co-contamination by antibiotics, heavy metals, and microplastics. Beyond mapping research trends, this review constructs a three-tier mitigation framework spanning extracellular DNA deconstruction and sequestration, MGE-mediated transfer inhibition, and system-level microecological restructuring through source management and soil amendment. Future work should integrate absolute gene loads, host identity, ARG-MGE linkage, transfer frequency, soil biogeochemical context, and field-scale ecological rebound into mechanistically grounded and ecologically defensible evaluation frameworks that assess reductions in ARG dissemination risk alongside effects on soil function, ecological resilience, and organic resource circularity.

title: Hybrid genome assemblies of Bacteroidota isolates uncover mobile genetic elements, antimicrobial resistance genes, and novel antimicrobial peptides
abstract: Members of the phylumdominate the mammalian gut microbiota and represent promising candidates for next-generation probiotics. However, the resolution of completegenomes is often hindered by extensive repetitive sequences and mobile genetic elements, a technical challenge further exacerbated by high intraspecies diversity and strain-level variants that drive assembly fragmentation and preclude the recovery of contiguous scaffolds. We recently isolated 18 strains that belonged to theorder offrom mouse ceca, human feces, and tortoise stool, which we now sequenced using both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms. We developed a specialized assembly workflow to reconstruct high-resolution genomes and characterize their extrachromosomal landscapes. The hybrid pipeline yielded 2 fully closed, single-contig chromosomes, 10 almost closed genomes, and 6 draft assemblies. Genomic integrity was exceptionally high, with completeness scores ranging from 99.6% to 100% and contamination levels below 2%. A total of 12 circular plasmids were detected across 10 isolates; eight isolates harbored a single plasmid, while two isolates (241163E and 241171E) each carried two distinct circular plasmids. Seven of these plasmids were experimentally confirmed through isolation and sequencing, and five were classified as viral contigs. Functional annotation revealed a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes and identified several predicted antimicrobial peptides in the assemblies through machine-learning analysis, of which two selected ones were experimentally verified. Overall, the resulting assemblies provide a reliable foundation for tracking mobile genetic elements, assessing resistance potential, and mining bioactive peptides inspecies intended for therapeutic development. Bacteria in the phylumare essential to mammalian gut health and are currently being developed as advanced probiotics. However, their complex DNA often prevents scientists from mapping their complete genetic blueprints, which can leave hidden traits like antibiotic resistance undetected. In this study, we combined two advanced DNA sequencing methods to create highly accurate and complete genetic maps for 18isolates from humans, mice, and tortoise. We successfully uncovered small, elusive DNA rings (potential plasmids) and confirmed their physical presence in the laboratory. Furthermore, we identified genes responsible for antibiotic resistance and used artificial intelligence to discover new antimicrobial peptides. This research provides a crucial foundation for the scientific community to accurately track mobile genes, rigorously evaluate the safety of potential gut therapeutics, and discover novel molecules for medical applications.

title: Stimuli-Responsive Copper Modified Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles as Smart Antimicrobial Delivery System for Antimicrobial Applications
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens poses a significant challenge to conventional antimicrobial therapies and underscores the urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies using highly efficacious and less toxic antimicrobial compounds, as well as more targeted antimicrobial delivery strategies to prevent uncontrolled release, which contributes to the rise of drug resistance. In this study, the design and synthesis of copper-modified mesoporous silica nanoparticles (Cu-MSNs) were described as a stimuli-responsive, smart antimicrobial delivery system incorporating carvacrol as a bioactive alternative to conventional antibiotics. The Cu-MSNs exhibit high surface area, tunable pore size, and efficient carvacrol loading. Copper ions embedded within the silica matrix provide intrinsic antimicrobial activity and may enhance the antimicrobial effect of carvacrol. Poly(2-(dimethylamino) ethyl methacrylate) (PDMAEMA) brushes were anchored on Cu-MSNs via surface-initiated atom transfer radical polymerization (SI-ATRP). The PDMAEMA brushes provided stimuli-responsive behavior, enabling pH- and temperature-dependent modulation of carvacrol release. The successful synthesis of Cu-MSN-PDMAEMA has been confirmed by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), elemental analysis (EA), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Moreover, stimuli-responsive behavior was confirmed using dynamic light scattering (DLS) experiments, demonstrating the pH- and temperature-dependent response of the PDMAEMA brushes. Finally, the carvacrol release behavior was studied at different pH values by using a sensitive paper-based electrochemical sensor. The multifunctional nanoplatform exhibited antimicrobial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as antiviral activity against representative enveloped and non-enveloped viral models. This synergistic design combines the benefits of a natural antimicrobial agent, intrinsic metallic activity, and smart polymer regulation, offering an strategy to enhance efficacy while minimizing off-target effects. Release studies demonstrated pH-triggered carvacrol delivery, with enhanced release under acidic conditions, confirming the gating function of the PDMAEMA brushes, highlighting the potential of these particles as an antibiotic-free alternative for preventing microbial infections while mitigating the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

title: Adjunctive Use of Azithromycin to Non-Surgical Periodontal Therapy: Rationale and Evidence for Its Use in Periodontitis-A Scoping Review
abstract: Antimicrobials are added as adjuncts to non-surgical periodontal therapy in certain cases to achieve improved outcomes. Among the adjunct antimicrobials that have gained renewed interest is azithromycin, owing to its additional anti-inflammatory and host-modulating properties. This review aims to summarise the pharmacology, adverse effects, and the current evidence for the adjunct use of azithromycin in different forms of periodontitis. In vitro studies, randomized controlled trials, and longitudinal studies published in English were searched in MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar (https://osf.io/m8enj/overview). Following screening of 677 articles, 70 articles were subjected to full-text review and ultimately 57 articles were included. In vitro studies demonstrated anti-bacterial, host-modulating, and anti-inflammatory properties of azithromycin with drug concentrating in inflamed tissues. The additional benefits of adjunctive azithromycin are moderate and inconsistent, although deep periodontal pockets may show enhanced improvements. Local delivery of azithromycin demonstrated additional benefits in single-rooted teeth. Azithromycin may provide clinical and microbiological benefits, especially in deep periodontal pockets. However, the World Health Organization categorizes azithromycin as a critically important antimicrobial for human medicine. Due to inconsistent results and owing to the importance of azithromycin, the adjunctive use of azithromycin with non-surgical periodontal therapy is currently not recommended.

title: gcPathogen 2.0: an expanded multi-omics database advancing global pathogen surveillance and One Health research
abstract: Launched in 2024, gcPathogen established a critical foundation for the genomic surveillance of human pathogens. Here, we present gcPathogen 2.0, a major multi-omics update designed to address key analytical bottlenecks, including the integration of genomic and transcriptional profiles, systematic tracking of cross-habitat distribution, and large-scale discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This release expands coverage from 1134 to 1506 pathogenic species, spanning 557 bacteria, 508 fungi, 258 viruses, and 183 parasites, and increases total genomic records past 2.3 million. By incorporating 12 597 transcriptomes across 148 species, gcPathogen 2.0 bridges the gap between gene carriage and functional expression for risk assessment. Furthermore, the platform integrates 285 925 pathogen metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) spanning human, animal, and environmental niches. Mapped across 68 Environment Ontology (ENVO) habitat categories, these MAGs enable comprehensive tracking of cross-habitat distribution of pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Leveraging a nonredundant reference set curated from seven public databases, we identified over 77 million AMPs belonging to >55 000 families across 438 bacterial pathogens. Finally, pan-genome analyses of 440 bacterial species map intraspecies functional distributions across core, accessory, and unique gene repertoires. gcPathogen 2.0 is publicly accessible at https://nmdc.cn/gcpathogen/.

title: PrEP, resistance and new clinical scenarios, DoxyPEP
abstract: HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a highly effective intervention to reduce HIV acquisition. However, the sustained rise in bacterial STIs highlights the need for preventive strategies beyond HIV. Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP) reduces syphilis andin selected populations. Its effect against gonorrhea is lower and depends on local resistance patterns. Because of its potential impact on antimicrobial resistance, DoxyPEP should be implemented with microbiological surveillance. PrEP and DoxyPEP should be integrated as complementary tools within a broader sexual health model.

title: Management of non-fermenting Gram-negative bacteria in critically ill patients focused on carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
abstract: Infections caused by non-fermenting Gram-negative bacteria represent a major therapeutic challenge. Their clinical management is associated with high morbidity and mortality, especially in immunocompromised or critically ill patients. This review aims to provide an overview focusing on microbiological characteristics, particularly those related with antimicrobial resistance, and the therapeutic approach, including novel available treatment options against infections caused by carbapenem-resistantandin critical care patients.

title: The changing epidemiology of multidrug-resistant bacteria in hospitals: from high-risk clones to clinical impact
abstract: Multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) have become a major challenge for healthcare systems, representing a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections worldwide. The hospital environment provides ideal conditions for the emergence and dissemination of these microorganisms due to intensive antimicrobial use, the concentration of vulnerable patients, frequent invasive procedures, and opportunities for cross-transmission. The epidemiology of MDRB is dynamic and varies according to geographic region, healthcare practices, and local antimicrobial selective pressure. This review briefly summarizes the current epidemiology of MDRB in hospital settings, focusing on the ESKAPE pathogens. Special attention is given to the emergence and international dissemination of the so-called high-risk clones, which have played a central role in the global spread of antimicrobial resistance. The review also addresses the principal epidemiological risk factors, transmission routes, the role of environmental reservoirs and colonized patients, and the contribution of intensive care units as major amplification points for MDRB transmission and maintenance. Moreover, infections caused by MDRB are associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and higher healthcare costs. Continuous surveillance, rapid microbiological diagnosis, infection prevention and control measures, and antimicrobial stewardship programs remain essential to limit their spread and clinical impact. New genomic surveillance approaches are improving our understanding of transmission dynamics and supporting more potentially effective control strategies.

title: Matrix-specific oxidant demand shapes antibiotic and antimicrobial resistance mitigation during wastewater ozonation
abstract: Ozonation is increasingly used for wastewater-based antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mitigation; however, how wastewater matrix complexity shapes simultaneous multiclass antibiotic degradation, bacterial inactivation, ARG degradation, and molecular determinants under realistic treatment conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study provides the first integrated matrix-dependent evaluation of multiclass antibiotic degradation, bacterial inactivation, ARGs degradation, and structure-reactivity relationships across actual WWTP effluent and controlled water matrices within a unified experimental framework. In WWTP effluent, ozonation completely removed 31 of 35 antibiotics while achieving > 99% viable bacterial reduction and > 97% ARGs reduction within 60 min. Matrix-dependent behavior was compound-class specific: amphenicols, nitroimidazoles, and β-lactams were highly sensitive to matrix composition, whereas tetracyclines and sulfonamides were largely unaffected. Lower pH selectively decreased degradation of fluoroquinolones and macrolides, highlighting the importance of pH-dependent speciation and intrinsic structural reactivity. Electronic susceptibility (HOMO) dominated in simple systems, whereas in complex matrices, interactions with dissolved organic matter (DOM) and bacterial components shifted control toward polarity, hydrophobicity, and polarizability, highlighting matrix-dependent determinants of antibiotic degradation. Critically, antibiotic residues minimally affected bacterial inactivation in actual WWTP effluent but significantly inhibited 16S rRNA and ARG degradation; whereas under simplified bacteria-containing PBS, they suppressed both processes because of stronger oxidant competition. DOM imposed immediate inhibition, whereas antibiotics caused persistent oxidant demand, jointly constraining ARGs removal. These findings demonstrate that conventional treatment endpoints may overestimate true AMR hazard reduction, as ARGs persistence remains more vulnerable to matrix-specific oxidant competition. Together, these findings establish matrix-specific oxidant demand as a mechanistic basis for optimizing ozone-based AMR mitigation.
